title: Autonomous equations and phase-line stability
terms: autonomous differential equation; equilibrium solution; stable equilibrium; asymptotic stability; unstable equilibrium; phase line.

exposition.text:
′
An autonomous scalar equation has form y = f(y). Its equilibria are roots of f. A phase
line marks the sign of f between successive roots: positive means solutions move upward and
negative means downward. An equilibrium is stable if solutions starting sufficiently close stay
close for future time; it is asymptotically stable if they also tend to the equilibrium.
′
For f continuously differentiable, f (a) < 0 implies asymptotic stability of an equilibrium a,
′ ′
and f (a) > 0 implies instability. If f (a) = 0, inspect the sign directly; the derivative test is
inconclusive. Under uniqueness, distinct solution curves do not cross, so a solution cannot pass
through an equilibrium. A one-sided attracting point need not be stable from both sides.

question.text:
′
For y = y(y − 1)(y − 2), which equilibria are asymptotically stable?
(A) 0 only (B) 1 only (C) 2 only (D) 0 and 2 only (E) All three

solution.text:
The sign alternates across the simple roots: negative below 0, positive on (0, 1), negative on
(1, 2), and positive above 2. Arrows point toward 1 from both sides and away from 0 and 2.

question.text:
′ 2
The solution of y = y (1 − y) with y(0) = −1 has what limit as t → ∞?
(A) −∞
(B) −1
(C) 0
(D) 1
(E) It reaches 0 in finite time and then ceases to exist.

solution.text:
For y < 0, the derivative is positive. Uniqueness prevents crossing the equilibrium 0, so
the solution increases and is bounded above. It exists for all future time while remaining in
[−1, 0]. Its limit must be an equilibrium, hence is 0. The equilibrium is attracting from the
left but repelling from the right.

question.text:
′ 3 ′ 3
For the two scalar equations y = −y and z = z , how is the equilibrium zero classified,
respectively?
(A) Unstable; unstable.
(B) Asymptotically stable; unstable.
(C) Stable but not asymptotically stable; asymptotically stable.
(D) Asymptotically stable; asymptotically stable.
(E) The vanishing derivatives at zero prevent any conclusion.

solution.text:
For the first equation, the derivative points toward zero on either side. Solutions remain
between their initial value and zero and converge to zero, so the equilibrium is asymptoti-
cally stable. For the second, the arrows point away on both sides; any nonzero initial value
eventually leaves a fixed small neighborhood. Both linearized derivatives vanish, so the sign
analysis supplies information that linearization does not.

question.text:
An autonomous equation has a continuously differentiable right side satisfying f (y) = 0 for
every y ∈ [−1, 1]. Which statement about the equilibrium zero is forced?
(A) It is unstable.
(B) It is asymptotically stable.
(C) It is stable but not asymptotically stable.
(D) Every solution starting outside [−1, 1] converges to zero.
(E) Every solution starting near zero leaves [−1, 1].

solution.text:
Every initial value sufficiently near zero lies in [−1, 1], and uniqueness makes its solu-
tion constant. Such solutions remain arbitrarily close to zero, giving stability. A nonzero
constant solution, however close its initial value, never converges to zero, so asymptotic
stability fails. The behavior outside this interval is irrelevant.

question.text:
If f : R → R is continuously differentiable, which statement must hold for every periodic
′
solution of y = f(y)?
(A) Its period is at least one.
(B) Its mean over a period is zero.
(C) It crosses an equilibrium twice in each period.
(D) It is constant.
(E) Its derivative never vanishes.

solution.text:
′
A periodic differentiable solution attains a maximum at some time t , where y (t ) = 0.
0 0
Thus its value a = y(t ) satisfies f(a) = 0. The constant solution y = a passes through
0
the same initial value. Local uniqueness, continued along the connected time domain,
forces the proposed periodic solution to be that constant. This is the scalar autonomous
no-crossing principle in a global form.
